# How do we describe [data]{.alert}?

## How do we describe [data]{.alert}?

- Why do we make the choices we make in describing data?
- These choices get bundled into knowledge system
- Whose knowledge system(s) do we learn and why?

## Learning Objectives

1. Describe the *location* of numerical variables using the [mean]{.alert} and [median]{.alert}
2. Describe the *spread* of numerical variables using the [standard deviation]{.alert}, [variance]{.alert}, [coefficient of variation]{.alert}, and [interquartile range]{.alert}
3. Describe categorical variables using the [proportion]{.alert}
4. Know when to use different descriptive statistics

## Describing location and spread of numerical data

**the Mean describes location**

| Descriptor | Parameter | Estimate | Units |
|------------|-----------|----------|-------|
| mean | $\mu$ | $\bar{Y}$ | measurement unit (e.g. cm, seconds, etc.) |

Notes:

- $\mu$ is Greek letter pronounced like "mew"
- $\bar{Y}$ pronounced like "Y bar"

## [Sample mean]{.alert}

In words:

> The [sample mean]{.alert} is the sum of all the observations in a sample divided by $n$, the number of observations

In math:

$$\bar{Y} = \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^{n} Y_i}{n}$$

## Describing location and spread of numerical data

**the Standard Deviation describes spread**

| Descriptor | Parameter | Estimate | Units |
|------------|-----------|----------|-------|
| mean | $\mu$ | $\bar{Y}$ | measurement unit |
| standard deviation | $\sigma$ | $s$ | measurement unit |

Notes:

- $\sigma$ ("sig-ma") is Greek letter "s"

## [Sample standard deviation]{.alert}

In words:

> The [standard deviation]{.alert} is a common measure of the spread of data. It indicates how far the different measurements are (on average) from the mean.

In math:

$$
\begin{aligned}
s^2 &= \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^{n} (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}{n - 1} \\
s &= \sqrt{s^2}
\end{aligned}
$$

$s^2$ is the sample variance

Take square root to get standard deviation: $\sqrt{s^2} = s$

## [Sample standard deviation]{.alert}

**FAQ**

Q1: Why does the sum of squared deviations ($\sum_{i = 1}^{n} (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2$) appear in the numerator?

A1: Negative and positive deviations have the same effect on average deviation. For example, suppose $\bar{Y} = 0$:

$$(1 - 0) ^ 2 = (1) ^ 2 = 1$$
$$(-1 - 0) ^ 2 = (-1) ^ 2 = 1$$

## [Sample standard deviation]{.alert}

**FAQ**

Q2: Why use the sum of squared deviations rather than absolute deviations?

A2: The squared values turn out to have better statistical properties than absolute values.

## [Sample standard deviation]{.alert}

**FAQ**

Q3: Why is it divided by $n-1$ rather than $n$?

A3: Dividing by $n$ is [biased]{.alert} and *underestimates* the population standard deviation. Matters most when $n$ is small.

## [Sample standard deviation]{.alert}

$$s^2 = \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^{n} (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}{n - 1} = \frac{6.3188}{7} = 0.9027~\mathrm{mm}^2$$

::: {.cell}

:::


$$s = \sqrt{0.9027} = 0.9501~\mathrm{mm}$$

The standard deviation has the same units as the measurements (mm in this case), so you can describe the departure from the mean in a consistent way.

"Almost 95% of data typically fall within two standard deviations of the mean"

## Describing location and spread of numerical data

**Coefficient of Variation is standard deviation as a percentage of the mean**

| Descriptor | Parameter | Estimate | Units |
|------------|-----------|----------|-------|
| mean | $\mu$ | $\bar{Y}$ | measurement unit |
| standard deviation | $\sigma$ | $s$ | measurement unit |
| variance | $\sigma^2$ | $s$ | measurement unit$^2$ |
| coefficient of variation | $\sigma/\mu \times 100\%$ | CV | percent (%) |

Notes:

- CV is useful for comparing data with different measurement units

## [Coefficient of variation]{.alert}

In words:

> The [coefficient of variation]{.alert} is the standard deviation expressed as a percentage of the mean

In math:

$$\mathrm{CV} = \frac{s}{\bar{Y}} \times 100\%$$

$$\mathrm{CV} = \frac{s}{\bar{Y}} \times 100\% = \frac{0.9501}{11.04} \times 100\% = 8.61 \%$$

## Describing location and spread of numerical data

 Descriptor | Parameter | Estimate | Units
------------|-----------|----------|-------
 median     | Median    | $M$      | measurement unit

Notes:

- "[median]{.alert} is the middle observation in a set of data"

## [Median]{.alert}

If $n$ is *odd*:

$$\text{Median} = Y_{([n+1]/2)}$$
If $n$ is *even*:

$$\text{Median} = [Y_{(n/2)} + Y_{(n/2+1)}]/2$$

## Median


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02-describing-data-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


$$n = 8$$

$$\text{Median} = \frac{Y_4 + Y_5}{2} = \frac{10.8 + 11.4}{2} = 11.10~\text{mm}$$

## Describing location and spread of numerical data

 Descriptor | Parameter | Estimate | Units
------------|-----------|----------|-------
 median     | Median    | $M$      | measurement unit
 interquartile range | Interquartile range    | $IQR$      | measurement unit

Notes:

- "[*IQR*]{.alert} is the difference between the third and first quartiles of the data. It is the span of the middle 50% of the data."

## Interquartile range


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02-describing-data-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


$$j = 0.25 n = 0.25 \times 8 = 2$$

$$\text{First quartile} = \frac{Y_2 + Y_3}{2} = \frac{10.6 + 10.6}{2} = 10.60~\text{mm}$$

## Interquartile range


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02-describing-data-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


$$k = 0.75 n = 0.75 \times 8 = 6$$

$$\text{Third quartile} = \frac{Y_{6} + Y_{7}}{2} = \frac{11.6 + 12}{2} = 11.80~\text{mm}$$

## Interquartile range


::: {.cell}

:::


$$\text{Interquartile range} = \text{Third quartile} - \text{First quartile} = 1.20~\text{mm}$$

$$\mathit{IQR} = 11.80 - 10.60 = 1.20~\text{mm}$$

## 3. Describe categorical variables using the [proportion]{.alert}

 Descriptor | Parameter | Estimate | Units
------------|-----------|----------|-------
 proportion     | proportion    | $\hat{p}$      | probability

Notes:

- the [sample proportion]{.alert} is similar to the [sample mean]{.alert}

## [Sample proportion]{.alert}

In words:

> The [sample proportion]{.alert} is a measure of the **location** of categorical data. It indicates how frequently a specific category is found in the data.

In math:

$$
\hat{p} = \frac{N_{[Y = \text{category}]}}{n}
$$

## [Sample proportion]{.alert}

Heads or tails?

`H T T T H H T H T T`

$$

## 4. Know when to use different descriptive statistics

When data are roughly symmetrical and there are not many extreme values

- mean, standard deviation, variance are commonly used
- CV if you want to compare values on different scales

When data are skewed and/or there are many extreme values

- median tells more about a typical unit in the population and is less sensitive to extreme values
- IQR is less sensitive to extreme values than standard deviation

## Rounding

* No standard rules
* For this class, round to 2 decimal places

  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
